Lecture 27

Laplace inversion by complex integration

Lecture objectives

We prove the uniqueness of the Laplace transform and derive the Bromwich inversion formula from Fourier inversion, with its limit and its values at jumps. We evaluate the inversion integral by closing the contour around poles and around a branch cut, and we check each inverse by its causal support, its initial and late behaviour and its forward transform.

Lecture 26 computed Laplace transforms only in the forward direction, from a signal to its transform. Solving an initial-value problem by transforms needs the opposite step: the algebra produces a transform F,FF, and we want the signal f.ff. This lecture first proves that a transform determines its signal, so that a table may be read from right to left. It then recovers the signal by an integral of estF(s)\ee^{st}F(s)estF(s) along a vertical line, which comes from the Fourier inversion theorems of Lecture 23. Finally it evaluates that integral by the residues and contours of Lectures 19 and 20. The lecture reads in three stages: uniqueness and the inversion integral (Sections 27.1 and 27.2), closing the contour (Sections 27.3–27.5), and checks on an inverse with a branch cut that leads to the diffusion kernel (Sections 27.6 and 27.7).

27.1 Uniqueness of the transform

We use the class of Lecture 26. A function fff on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) is piecewise continuous if on every bounded subinterval of (0,∞),(0,\infty)(0,∞), including intervals (0,β],(0,\beta](0,β], it is continuous except at finitely many points, with finite one-sided limits there. So its exceptional points do not accumulate at 0,00, although fff itself may be unbounded near 0.00. It is transformable at a real number ccc if ∫0∞e−ct∣f(t)∣ ⁣dt<∞,\int_0^\infty\ee^{-ct}\abs{f(t)}\dd t<\infty∫0∞​e−ct∣f(t)∣dt<∞, and cfc_fcf​ is its abscissa of absolute convergence. Its transform F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t) ⁣dtF(s)=\int_0^\infty\ee^{-st}f(t)\dd tF(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt is analytic on the half-plane Re⁡s>cf\Re s>c_fRes>cf​ (Lecture 26).

27.2 The Bromwich integral

On a vertical line in its half-plane the Laplace transform is a Fourier transform (Lecture 26). Lecture 23 inverted Fourier transforms, so we obtain an inversion formula for Laplace transforms. We need the class of Lecture 23 on the half-line. A function fff on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) is piecewise C1C^1C1 on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) if every bounded interval [0,β][0,\beta][0,β] has a finite partition such that on each open piece fff is differentiable and fff and f′f'f′ extend continuously to the closed piece. The formula (27.2) is the Bromwich integral, also called the Riemann–Mellin formula. We read it as follows.

  • The limit is symmetric. The same cutoff RRR is used above and below the real axis, as in Lecture 23. For a signal with a jump, the two one-sided improper integrals need not converge separately: for F=1/s,F=1/sF=1/s, c>0c>0c>0 and t=0t=0t=0 the segment integral is π−1arctan⁡(R/c)→12,\pi^{-1}\arctan(R/c)\to\tfrac12π−1arctan(R/c)→21​, while over [c−iR1,c+iR2][c-\iu R_1,c+\iu R_2][c−iR1​,c+iR2​] its imaginary part −ln⁡((c2+R22)/(c2+R12))/(4π)-\ln\bigl((c^2+R_2^2)/(c^2+R_1^2)\bigr)/(4\pi)−ln((c2+R22​)/(c2+R12​))/(4π) has no limit.

  • Values at jumps. At a jump the formula gives the half-sum of the one-sided limits, not the value of f,ff, which the transform does not determine. At t=0t=0t=0 it gives 12f(0+),\tfrac12f(0^+)21​f(0+), because the causal signal jumps from 000 to f(0+)f(0^+)f(0+) there, and for t<0t<0t<0 it gives 0.00.

27.3 Closing the contour: poles

In the second stage we evaluate the Bromwich integral by residues. As in Lecture 19, we close the segment by an arc, evaluate the closed integral by residues and show that the arc contributes nothing in the limit. For t>0t>0t>0 the factor est\ee^{st}est is small where Re⁡s\Re sRes is very negative, so we close to the left. For R>0R>0R>0 let ARleftA^{\mathrm{left}}_RARleft​ be the semicircle with centre ccc and radius RRR that runs from c+iRc+\iu Rc+iR through c−Rc-Rc−R to c−iR,c-\iu Rc−iR, and let ARrightA^{\mathrm{right}}_RARright​ be the semicircle that runs from c−iRc-\iu Rc−iR through c+Rc+Rc+R to c+iRc+\iu Rc+iR (Figure 27.1). The segment followed by ARleftA^{\mathrm{left}}_RARleft​ is a closed path around the left half-disc. The segment followed by ARrightA^{\mathrm{right}}_RARright​ traversed backwards, from c+iRc+\iu Rc+iR to c−iR,c-\iu Rc−iR, is a closed path around the right half-disc.

For rational transforms the residues give the signal directly, by partial fractions and the forward transforms of Lecture 26.

Summary

A Laplace transform determines its signal up to values at finitely many points in each bounded interval, and a signal with impulses including its impulses. On a vertical line Re⁡s=c\Re s=cRes=c the Laplace transform is the Fourier transform of e−ctf(t),\ee^{-ct}f(t)e−ctf(t), so Fourier inversion with symmetric cutoffs gives the Bromwich integral. Closing its segment to the left evaluates it by residues, provided the transform tends to zero on the arcs; Jordan’s estimate handles the factor est\ee^{st}est separately.

  • Uniqueness: F=GF=GF=G on a real ray s>s0s>s_0s>s0​ implies f=gf=gf=g at every t>0t>0t>0 where f−gf-gf−g is continuous; impulses are determined too.

  • Bromwich: for fff piecewise C1C^1C1 on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) and transformable at c,cc, the limit as R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞ of (2πi)−1∫c−iRc+iRestF ⁣ds(2\pi\iu)^{-1}\int_{c-\iu R}^{c+\iu R}\ee^{st}F\dd s(2πi)−1∫c−iRc+iR​estFds is 12(f(t+)+f(t−))\tfrac12(f(t^+)+f(t^-))21​(f(t+)+f(t−)) for t>0,t>0t>0, 12f(0+)\tfrac12f(0^+)21​f(0+) at t=0t=0t=0 and 000 for t<0.t<0t<0.

  • Residues: with finitely many singular points left of the line and max⁡ARleft∣F∣→0,\max_{A^{\mathrm{left}}_R}\abs F\to0maxARleft​​∣F∣→0, the half-sum equals ∑jRes⁡s=sj(estF)\sum_j\Res_{s=s_j}(\ee^{st}F)∑j​Ress=sj​​(estF) for t>0;t>0t>0; for rational FFF the residue sum is the continuous inverse.

  • Closures: e−asG:\ee^{-as}Ge−asG: close left for t>a,t>at>a, right for t<a;t<at<a; for a periodic signal the residues are its Fourier coefficients; e−xs/D/(2Ds):\ee^{-x\sqrt{s/D}}/(2\sqrt{Ds})e−xs/D​/(2Ds​): a cut along (−∞,0](-\infty,0](−∞,0] gives e−x2/(4Dt)/4πDt.\ee^{-x^2/(4Dt)}/\sqrt{4\pi Dt}e−x2/(4Dt)/4πDt​.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Two causal signals of the lecture’s transformable class have equal Laplace transforms on a common right half-plane. Each signal consists of a regular part and finitely many impulses at distinct times with nonzero weights. What does uniqueness imply?

Hint. Compare the cumulative signals obtained by integrating once, and use the transform convention at zero.

Dividing the transform difference by sss on a sufficiently far-right half-plane gives the transform of the cumulative difference. By uniqueness for ordinary signals, this cumulative function vanishes except possibly at finitely many points in each bounded interval. Its jumps give the differences in impulse weights. Both one-sided limits vanish at positive times. At the initial instant the left limit is zero by causality and the right limit is zero by uniqueness. Thus every jump is zero. Between impulses the cumulative function is continuous and therefore zero on the whole interval. Differentiating there gives zero for the difference of the regular parts at their continuity points. Changing an assigned point value leaves the integral unchanged, while the transform includes the full weight of an impulse at zero.

2. A causal signal equals 4e−t4\ee^{-t}4e−t for t>0t>0t>0 and has no impulses. What value does the symmetric Bromwich integral give at t=0t=0t=0 for F(s)=4/(s+1)F(s)=4/(s+1)F(s)=4/(s+1), along a line Re⁡s=c\Re s=cRes=c with c>−1c>-1c>−1? Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. After shifting to a Fourier inverse, what are the two one-sided limits of the weighted causal signal at zero?

The weighted signal e−ctf(t)\ee^{-ct}f(t)e−ctf(t) has one-sided limits 000 and 444 at zero. Symmetric Fourier inversion gives their half-sum (0+4)/2=2(0+4)/2=2(0+4)/2=2. The factor restoring the weight is ect=1\ee^{ct}=1ect=1 at zero, so the Bromwich value is also 222. The full right limit would ignore the causal zero extension on the left.

3. For t>0t>0t>0, invert F(s)=1/(s+2)2F(s)=1/(s+2)^2F(s)=1/(s+2)2 along the Bromwich line Re⁡s=0\Re s=0Res=0. Which expression does the contour method give?

Hint. Close where the exponential is bounded and use the residue rule for a double pole.

For t>0t>0t>0 the left semicircle has ∣est∣≤1\abs{\ee^{st}}\le1∣est∣≤1, and FFF is O(R−2)O(R^{-2})O(R−2) there by the reverse triangle inequality. Its arc integral tends to zero. The upward line and left arc give positive orientation. At the double pole s=−2s=-2s=−2, the residue is the first derivative of est\ee^{st}est at −2-2−2, hence te−2tt\ee^{-2t}te−2t. Treating the pole as simple loses the factor ttt. Reversing the orientation changes the sign, and closing right to get zero does not give the required arc decay.

4. For the causal signal f(t)=sin⁡tf(t)=\sin tf(t)=sint for t>0t>0t>0, its transform is F(s)=1/(s2+1)F(s)=1/(s^2+1)F(s)=1/(s2+1) on Re⁡s>0\Re s>0Res>0. The limit of sF(s)sF(s)sF(s) as real s→0+s\to0^+s→0+ is zero. What does this say about the late-time signal?

Hint. Check which limit the final-value proposition assumes before relating the two quantities.

The sine keeps oscillating and has no limit as time grows. The proposition assumes that time limit before identifying it with the limit of sF(s)sF(s)sF(s). Positive real sss can approach zero inside the transform half-plane, so that transform limit is valid. The proposition concerns sF(s)sF(s)sF(s) and gives no final value from the formula’s value at zero.
